If calf exam (a7) has not yet been performed, DVT-signs points cannot be scored and this item should be run after a7/a8.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Suspected pulmonary embolism with concurrent left lower extremity DVT, high clinical probability (Wells score ~7.5)
differential: Pulmonary embolism (most likely given DVT signs, pleuritic pain, hypoxia, tachycardia, hemoptysis)
Deep vein thrombosis with reactive pleurisy (less likely given hypoxia and tachycardia severity)
Musculoskeletal chest pain from prolonged driving posture (does not explain hypoxia or leg findings)
Pneumonia (less likely, no fever/cough, but cannot fully exclude without imaging)
Pneumothorax (less likely given no trauma history, but pleuritic pain and dyspnea warrant consideration until imaging excludes)
keyFindings: Pleuritic right-sided chest pain since this morning
Dyspnea on exertion, winded climbing one flight of stairs
Home SpO2 93% on room air, pulse 112
Left calf swelling, tenderness, and redness x5 days after prolonged car travel
Calf circumference asymmetry (39 cm vs 34.5 cm)
Wells score high probability for PE
No fever, no documented prior VTE or malignancy
plan: Do NOT prescribe outpatient antibiotics; this is not a presentation consistent with bacterial pneumonia and antibiotics will not address the suspected PE/DVT
Advise patient this requires emergency in-person evaluation today, not a routine outpatient visit
Instruct patient to call 911 or have someone drive him immediately to the nearest emergency department given hypoxia, tachycardia, and high pretest probability of PE
Communicate urgency clearly: hemoptysis plus hypoxia plus leg swelling after prolonged immobility is a medical emergency

Address insurance/cost concern directly: emergency departments cannot refuse emergency care regardless of insurance status (EMTALA); do not let cost concerns delay care for a life-threatening condition
Do not discharge home or arrange routine follow-up; this is outside the scope of a telehealth disposition decision
Document Wells score and reasoning in ED-style note to communicate urgency to receiving facility
Advise against further long-distance driving until evaluated
If patient refuses to go, document informed refusal discussion and strongly re-emphasize risk, offer to call ambulance on his behalf
redFlags: Unilateral leg swelling/tenderness after prolonged immobility
educationPoints: Pleuritic chest pain plus unilateral leg swelling after prolonged travel should always trigger PE/DVT screening even without fever or cough
Home pulse oximetry and patient-performed exertional walk tests are valid, feasible teletriage tools to detect occult hypoxia
Hemoptysis is often minimized or withheld by patients out of fear; direct, nonjudgmental questioning increases disclosure
A request for 'just an antibiotic' should prompt the clinician to clarify the actual diagnosis being treated rather than acquiescing to patient preference
EMTALA guarantees emergency department screening and stabilization regardless of insurance or ability to pay; this should be explicitly communicated to allay cost-related reluctance to seek care
Telehealth disposition for suspected PE is virtual triage leading to immediate escalation (911/ED), not an outpatient diagnostic pathway, since CTPA cannot be obtained remotely

artifacts.body: 41-year-old male presenting with nasal congestion and sneezing during spring pollen season. No chronic medical conditions reported. No tobacco use. Works long hours as a rideshare driver. Denies prior surgeries, hospitalizations, or blood clots. Advised OTC antihistamine. Plan: follow up as needed.

artifacts.title: Wells Criteria Scoring Worksheet
artifacts.author: ED Resident, telehealth visit
artifacts.body:
Prerequisite: clinical signs/symptoms of DVT must be confirmed on exam (see guided calf inspection/palpation) before this item can be scored.
Clinical signs/symptoms of DVT (leg swelling + pain on palpation of deep veins), confirmed on exam: +3
PE is #1 diagnosis OR no alternative diagnosis as likely: +3
Heart rate >100: +1.5
Immobilization ≥3 days or surgery in previous 4 weeks: 0 — note: standard Wells wording requires bed rest/immobilization ≥3 days or surgery within 4 weeks; two days of prolonged car travel (9 hours each way) does not meet this threshold and is not equivalent to the ≥3 day immobilization criterion, so it is not scored, though it remains a relevant VTE risk factor clinically
Previous objectively diagnosed PE or DVT: 0
Malignancy: 0
Hemoptysis: +1
Total (Wells, classic): 7.5 → High probability of PE (score >6)

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient reports drinking alcohol rarely, about once a month
mismatches.recordEvidence: Prior telehealth note from 6 months ago makes no mention of alcohol use being screened or documented either way
mismatches.teachingPoint: Absence of documentation is not evidence of absence; this is a distractor to test whether the learner inappropriately anchors on alcohol use as relevant to the current presentation rather than pursuing the DVT/PE history

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient requests an antibiotic and hopes to avoid in-person or emergency evaluation
mismatches.recordEvidence: Wells Criteria Scoring Worksheet documents a score of 7.5, indicating high probability of PE requiring emergent CT pulmonary angiogram, not an antibiotic or outpatient management
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patient treatment preferences and cost concerns, while important to acknowledge empathetically, cannot override objective clinical risk stratification indicating a life-threatening diagnosis requiring emergency care

objectives.text: Elicit a focused history that uncovers both the pulmonary (pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, hemoptysis) and vascular (unilateral leg swelling after prolonged travel) components of the presentation despite the patient's initial reluctance to volunteer the leg symptoms and hemoptysis

Use remote-appropriate assessment tools (home pulse oximeter, guided pulse/respiratory rate counts, exertional walk observation, guided calf measurement) to objectively characterize severity when in-person vitals and exam are unavailable

Correctly calculate and interpret a Wells score to risk-stratify for pulmonary embolism and recognize that a high-probability score mandates same-day CT pulmonary angiogram, which cannot be obtained via telehealth

Recognize and name the mismatch between the patient's framing of the problem (wants an antibiotic, hopes to avoid the ED) and the objective clinical picture (hypoxia, tachycardia, high Wells score) documented in the chart

Formulate an emergency disposition plan appropriate to this role's scope: direct the patient to activate emergency services or go immediately to an in-person ED for CT pulmonary angiogram, rather than prescribing antibiotics or arranging routine outpatient follow-up

Address the patient's financial and logistic concerns about emergency care (uninsured status, fear of losing driving income) with accurate information about emergency care access (EMTALA) while maintaining urgency of the recommendation

patient.name: Bashir Rahimi
patient.appearance: A man of average build in his early forties with short dark hair and a trimmed beard, wearing a plain gray t-shirt, seated on a couch in a modestly furnished living room with a ceiling fan visible overhead. He appears anxious and mildly short of breath, occasionally shifting position and glancing away from the camera, with a phone propped against a stack of books.

persona.personality: Hardworking, stoic, and somewhat guarded about health concerns, tends to minimize symptoms until directly reassured it's safe to share them
persona.communicationStyle: Polite and cooperative but gives brief initial answers; opens up with gentle, specific follow-up questions and reassurance; occasionally deflects to practical concerns about work and money
persona.emotionalState: Anxious beneath a calm exterior, worried about both his health and the financial impact of missing work or incurring medical bills
persona.background: Bashir immigrated to the US as a young adult and has worked various jobs before settling into rideshare driving eight years ago. He supports himself and sends money to family periodically, works long hours by choice to maximize earnings, and has avoided routine healthcare due to lack of insurance and tight finances.
speechExamples: It's not that bad, I can handle it, I just wanted to check before it gets worse.
Honestly, I was hoping to avoid going anywhere today if I could help it.
I didn't want to make a big deal out of the leg thing, I figured it would go away.
If I can't work tonight, that's a problem, but I guess health comes first... I hope this isn't serious.
concerns: Worried about the cost of going to an emergency room without insurance
Concerned about losing income if he cannot drive
Hoping for a quick fix like antibiotics rather than a more involved workup
Underlying fear that this could be something serious given the blood in his cough

scenario.studentBrief: You are an emergency medicine resident conducting a virtual urgent care visit. Bashir Rahimi, a 41-year-old rideshare driver, has requested a telehealth visit for sharp right-sided chest pain worse with deep breathing, and shortness of breath climbing stairs, since this morning. Gather a focused history, use remote assessment tools available to you, and determine the appropriate disposition.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Sharp right-sided chest pain worse with deep breathing, and shortness of breath climbing stairs, since this morning
scenario.openingLine: Hi doctor, thanks for seeing me. My chest has been hurting since this morning, kind of sharp, and I got winded just going up one flight of stairs at home, which isn't normal for me.
tasks: Take a focused history of the presenting concern
Use remote-appropriate tools to assess vital signs and functional status
Apply an appropriate clinical decision tool to guide your assessment
Communicate a clear disposition recommendation and address the patient's concerns
Document a focused note including history, examination findings, clinical reasoning, and disposition

profile.summary: A 41-year-old uninsured rideshare driver presents via telehealth with pleuritic chest pain and exertional dyspnea the morning after a long-distance drive, with reluctantly disclosed unilateral leg swelling and a single episode of hemoptysis. The case tests the resident's ability to elicit sensitive history, use remote assessment tools to risk-stratify for pulmonary embolism via Wells criteria, and deliver an urgent escalation-to-ED disposition despite the patient's preference for an antibiotic and reluctance to incur emergency care costs.
